name: Karlheinz Stockhausen
hook: The composer whose tape and electronic pieces reached rock through two routes: his own students, who founded Can, and the Beatles, who put his face on a record sleeve.
blurb: Stockhausen went to Paris in 1952 and made his first tape piece in Schaeffer's studio. Back in Cologne he worked at the radio station's electronic studio, the WDR studio, where he made Gesang der Jünglinge, a boy's singing voice cut up and mixed with electronic tones. That puts him between the two founding European electronic studios. He is here for his reach rather than for his concert works. He also taught: Holger Czukay studied with him from 1963 to 1966 and Irmin Schmidt went to his Cologne courses in 1964 and 1965, and the two went on to start Can. The Beatles listened to his records too, which is well documented, and his face is on the cover of Sgt. Pepper. At a press conference in Hamburg in 2001 he made remarks about the 11 September attacks that were widely reported and led to concerts being cancelled. He said afterwards that he had been misreported. That is recorded here as part of his public history, not as a judgement of the music.

signatureTracks.title: Gesang der Jünglinge
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: A child's voice cut into syllables and mixed with pure electronic tones. The Cologne studio's best-known piece.

signatureTracks.title: Hymnen
signatureTracks.whyThisOne: National anthems from around the world, heard through shortwave radio noise and tape. The critic Ian MacDonald suggested it as a model for the Beatles' 'Revolution 9'.
